The Washington Agreement between the Muslims and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, by which the MKF was created, and which was a very serious activity in re-building up the Bosnian Army, this could be seen in the weapons they had, or equipment, in Sarajevo and also the materiel that was brought into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were totally aware, then, that there was an embargo on the import of weapons to Bosnia and that the United Nations were fighting against that? Actually, they knew that this was in place; right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Americans were very clear about that with their policy of lift and strike -- lift the embargo and strike the Serbs. UNPROFOR did its very best to make clear that there were three parties in conflict that had to come to the table, but the Washington Agreement only invited two, with all -- to the table, with all of the consequences that we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here, you're talking about the infiltration of intelligence officers as liaison officers in humanitarian operations, and so on and so forth; then the presence of the CIA, who were employed in various ways. Are you familiar with the Dutch author --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- who said that different organisations, including humanitarian organisations, youth organisations, were massively infiltrated by various kinds of intelligence officers, and that Sarajevo was a kind of cradle of various intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with this representation of facts. UNPROFOR and UNHCR were neutral organisations. They distanced themselves from intelligence organisations, and they were not infiltrated; I do not think so. But there was an American contribution. We were able to see that. The Americans did very clearly have -- try to have a relationship with UNPROFOR. All other so-called infiltrations which have been claimed by journalists, I leave it to the journalists to bear responsibility for those claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next unmarked paragraph speaks specifically about the findings of the Dutch Institute, speaks about this infiltration. Do you agree that this was an additional reason for Serb caution in relation to these numerous non-governmental organisations and news teams?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As we go further and further, I find myself wondering what the relevance of this whole line of questioning is, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very gladly. First of all, the Serbian side was accused of acting, as it states in my indictment in 11 counts, particularly in Count 11, in a particular way. I would like to show to the parties, to the Trial Chamber, that the Serbian side had reasons for concern and for caution because a vast organisation was working on the defeat of the Serbian side, and this is evidence that we were fighting against an immeasurably greater force than us. And this fact, that those organisations were infiltrated, justifies our controls, inspections of convoys, and generally the caution in relation to the foreign presence at our lines and in our territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I don't think there's any difficulty with relevance. The concern of the Trial Chamber is whether or not this witness is going to be the witness who can best deal with the issues which you are raising.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellency, words of this witness are being interpreted right here, and his name is mentioned in this paragraph. This is not a question of Serbian paranoia. This is a matter of the massive presence of intelligence services, and those who were not favourable towards the Serbian side, at that, and this is something that the witness noted at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We can see what the witness noted, or we can see what is reported. I think the most efficient course, then, is simply ask the general whether he can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you think you can answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my name is linked to statements, I bear responsibility for them. The NIOD report was discussed in great detail. Observations made by the NIOD now, seven years later, looking back, establishing how various countries set up intelligence organisations, well, that is something that really I cannot comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just one further note, Your Honour. We don't agree that these extracts put to the general represent anything extracted from the NIOD report. In fact, if you look further through this document, Your Honour, it appears it may refer to private interviews. There's a large number of citations to confidential sources, confidential informants. And, frankly, Your Honour, if it was something from the NIOD report, it wouldn't be in this language, in the first instance, in any regard. So I just don't want the general to be under any misapprehension that these represent citations from the NIOD report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. Let me understand fully what you just stated. What is this? You said this is not an extract or excerpt of the NIOD report?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think this comes from a book, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The NIOD book?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I retrieved this. This is directly from the NIOD report. If you look at the top of the document, there's a citation to their web site, in which the report is published on the internet. And yesterday I went to that web site, and I looked at the different chapters and selected these ones in which General Van Baal has been quoted. And that NIOD report is available on-line as well as in hard copy, and I can assure you that everything that's been exhibited in this document comes verbatim from the NIOD report. And I think the general could confirm that, since he seems to be very familiar with that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear at the outset this is a sort of excerpt from that NIOD report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The report, itself, is in several volumes, it's hundreds of pages, and so these are excerpts that pertain to this particular subject that Dr. Karadzic wanted to question. But if the Chamber wishes, we could print out the entire report and we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I remember the general confirmed the part in which he was referred to, so we can safely move on. You have 10 minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 11, and then we will complete this particular section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, in paragraph 5, "UNPROFOR and DutchBat as a target for communications intelligence." And -- communication intelligence. And here, this part is where you are quoted as confirming that there was bugging, and so on and so forth; that this could have done by the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army. Ah, yes, there was a joke made here. General Rose made a joke here and confirmed that they were bugged, and that this was something that was accessible to the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a correct representation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I tender these parts of the document that refer to the witness? They are marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Given that the general has, without looking at what appears to be his transcripts of the original interviews, confirmed the accuracy of those excerpts, I would agree to those excerpts only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit only those parts confirmed by the witness and which refers to the general's statement at the time; i.e., the highlighted part.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D843, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I am now going to go back a little bit, about your knowledge about the military installations in Sarajevo. Is it correct that you said in one testimony that there was a large number of military installations in Sarajevo, as well as mobile targets such as military trucks, and so on and so forth? If you want me to remind you, you stated this in the Galic case on the 8th of July, 2002, on pages 11392 to 394. If you can confirm this, we don't need to call up the document.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I confirmed before does not need to be confirmed again. A large number of barracks and military trucks which were hidden or which were inside the barracks, these were seen. Weapons systems were not part of this, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you also said that they successfully placed mortars, let's say, close to the airport or other installations, and even a tank close to the Kosevo Hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two incidents took place, they're in my statement; one was a mortar near the airport and one a tank near the Kosevo Hospital, that's correct. As far as the weapon collection points are concerned, there was one at Tito Barracks, weapons under the control of the French. And for UNPROFOR, there was a place under the tunnel near the Olympic Stadium where UNPROFOR had no access to this, and it was said that heavy weapons had been there. I was not able to check and never had access to that tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You heard rumours that explosives were being manufactured near the Tito Barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We investigated this, but we found nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at Bosnalijek factory near the tunnel in Velesici, there was a production plant making explosives?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have confirmed that the majority of conflicts -- sparks and conflicts took place along the front-lines that went through the city. According to what you know, did these front-lines cross through the city at several different locations?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A recent map would be necessary from the period in order to show where the confrontation line actually ran and whether it is the case that it went through the city. It was the fact that in the northern part, the front-line was close to the houses and close to flat buildings. That is a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this line crossed over the buildings in Dobrinja, and that at Grbavica you had a street or a river that was a separation line between the two parties? Sometimes it was a street, sometimes a river.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time for you to wrap up your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you state that 99 per cent of the Serb heavy weaponry was under UNPROFOR control and that it was out of action?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 99 per cent of the Serbian heavy weaponry were under the control of UNPROFOR. That is more than surveillance, more than supervision, and they also were not -- most of them were not used. They were maintained -- it was trained with these, but they were, in general, not used. There were some exceptions during the period that I was chief of staff, where some weapons systems were withdrawn from control by UNPROFOR, and this was a violation of the Total Exclusion Zone regime, for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last topic, General, is as follows: Do you remember Silajdzic telling you that they were after a gold medal because they managed to portray themselves as victims to win over the sympathy of the international community and strong support of the USA, and that they were after a gold medal? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an almost correct representation of a private comment by Mr. Silajdzic which he made to me. It is not complete. I refer you back to my earlier statement about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In your opinion, what he meant by saying that they were after a gold medal, was that an explanation why they refused to accept peace and that, instead, they wanted the whole of Bosnia, they wanted to be victorious in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be wise to pose the question to Mr. Silajdzic, himself. I'm not going to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. Edgerton, how long would you need for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We started -- I think we can continue. Let's do it now. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, in your evidence yesterday, at page 8460, lines 13 to 17, you were asked: "Is it true that the tram was running parallel with the confrontation line and that it could have been hit from either side during the exchange of fire between them, especially in the area of Sniper Alley?" Your reply was: "Technically, it would have been possible to bring that about." Do you remember that question and giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave that answer, and I remember it clearly. It was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, first of all, when Dr. Karadzic referred to "either side" in his question, what did you understand him to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shooting at the trams from the BSA side or the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you gave your answer, did you have in mind any types of situations in particular?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I gave an answer as I intended. Technically, it was possible that Muslim military and Serbian military could shoot at the trams. That was my answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, over the course of your tour in Sarajevo, did you ever receive any reports or information to the effect that trams had been fired on by forces on the Bosnian-held side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw a report which showed that it had been established that a Bosnian military Muslim -- that a BiH military shot at the trams. I've never seen such a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, I have three questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have your statement in front of you. The first question relates to para 48 of your amalgamated statement. The second part of that paragraph reads like this: "I concluded that there was, indeed, a policy or a tactic employed by both the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the president side of using sniping as a means of repression and terror." I wonder whether you can expand on the tactics or policies adopted by the Bosnian side -- the president side of using sniping as a means of repression and terror.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the whole conflict, a large number of moments occurred in which there were casualties in Sarajevo because of sniping. In my contacts, beginning with the first conversation with General Milovanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The date the interpreter missed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... and the following discussions, I became more and more convinced that what was happening on the ground was, indeed, following on a command-and-control system from above and could be influenced in that direction. It had been -- they had tried many times to tell me that they could not have influence on what happened on the ground, but it became -- was shown -- demonstrated time and time again that that control was there. The direct influence being executed was shown many, many times. The arguments used in relation to this topic alarmed me. I realised that from 1994, when heavy weapons were no longer a way in which the city of Sarajevo could stay in its former situation, that an alternative, with small weapons at greater distance, in order to tell the civilians that we can determine what happens in the city, became a reality. I became convinced in my discussions with General Milovanovic that whatever he said was in harmony with what Mladic, his chief and the then president. I concluded that politically and at the highest military level, and at the level of execution, there was a clear line about using snipers. The role -- I say there was a unilateral role played by the Serbs. I deduced, from the context and the activities which were taking place, that this was the case. I have not said anything about the situation on the Bosnian side. I have no opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My question was rather focused on the president side, because you included the president side in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I deduced that primarily from my conversations with Victor Andreev and Krajisnik and the vice-president. If you probe more specifically, I'm not referring to the former president of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Karadzic, but Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it there. My second question relates to paragraphs from 22 to 26 or 7. You'll remember that the Canadian Battalion -- Canadian forces were surrounded by VRS members, and you telephoned Mr. Karadzic, and Karadzic agreed to tell them to withdraw, and, actually, they did. And you said it's an example of the command and control of Mr. Karadzic over the VRS members. Do you remember that, General Van Baal?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we also noted in your statement overnight that you found that VRS members installed the remote-controlled mines, so my question is that: Despite the order of Mr. Karadzic to withdraw, they installed those mines, so can one not say whether it's an example of the fact that his orders were not respected by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second situation -- first, let me state that I was unable to verify, regarding the situation in the evening and overnight, that the instructions went directly from Mr. Karadzic to the ground troops or who was the intermediary. That's one point. The second thing, as we discussed the next day, that Mr. Karadzic, through General Galic, expressed tremendous dissatisfaction that the remote-controlled mines had been placed again underneath the vehicles, and he promised that they would be removed. So the second time Karadzic told General Galic that the remote-controlled mines had to be removed from under the vehicles, and within 20 minutes from the Serb side and via my headquarters from Galic, we heard that that had, indeed, happened. So the remarks and instructions from Dr. Karadzic were being directly carried out at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, then I'll leave it there. My last question is related to the notes you admitted to have taken at the time. It transpired during the cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic's legal adviser, Mr. Robinson, that you indicated that you had contemporaneous notes from your time in Sarajevo, and you reviewed those notes prior to giving testimony in this case, and you, indeed, refreshed your memory, thanks to those notes. Since I note that the motion was filed by the Defence, and probably the Prosecution will have the opportunity to comment upon this, and then you were given the opportunity to respond to this, but it is the Chamber's practice to leave it in the voluntary co-operation between the parties and witness, so can I ask you, again, whether you would be prepared to disclose those parts which was taken during your tour in Sarajevo, redacting all those unnecessary or irrelevant parts? I remember you stated that -- I don't -- you didn't see any reason whatsoever to release them, but whether you are minded to reconsider your position.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll think about this, and I'll let you know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My last comment is that whether you would be prepared to copy those parts in particular that relate to your meeting with General Milovanovic, when he alleged, say, that he would see to it that trams would be targeted. So we'll ask our Victims and Witness Section to contact you after your testimony is over and whether -- I would appreciate it very much if you let us know about your position.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your testimony, General Van Baal. I thank you, on behalf of the Bench and the Tribunal, for your coming to the Tribunal to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for half an hour. No, we -- yes, we need to adjourn for half an hour, and we'll begin next in -- resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the next witness's evidence, shall we go into private session to discuss one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Miokovic. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. As discussed in our previous private session, given that the witness consents to lifting the protective measures, i.e., pseudonym, the Chamber grants the motion from the Defence to lift the protective measures being limited to the use of pseudonym. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I forgot to mention the Chamber also consulted the three Judges involved in the previous proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Miokovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You gave statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in November 1995 and February 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, only I really cannot tell you the exact dates. But I did give those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You testified in the trials of Dragomir Milosevic and Momcilo Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On Tuesday, which was the 26th of October, you reviewed a copy of an amalgamated statement which contains relevant parts from your earlier statements and testimony; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to make one or two corrections to that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for 65 ter 90198, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, Mr. Miokovic, do you see the first page of your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to clarify just one point concerning the sequence of events on the 8th of November, 1994. And this is at page 3 of your statement. No need for you to review it, Mr. Miokovic. But do you recall that after you finished your on-site investigation after the first shell had impacted, you waited at the site of the location, and -- do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were waiting at the site after we had completed the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you finished your on-site investigation at 4.55 p.m., and the second shell hit Livanjska Street at 5.25 p.m., just half an hour later. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you just clarify at what time you left Livanjska Street after completing the investigation into the first impact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Due to the fact that I wanted to wait for UNPROFOR members to arrive on the scene, as was the usual practice, and they were not coming, during which time the city was under heavy shelling, even the broader area, not only the place where I was, now my judgement was that I should wait for another 10 or 15 minutes, and after that I ordered all the evidence to be collected from the scene and that scene be abandoned. So, in hindsight, I think that this took place at around 10 past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, with that clarification, Your Honours, could I ask that the statement be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I propose to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. The witness was an investigator and an investigative team leader for the CSB Sarajevo, and in that capacity participated in investigations of shelling and sniping incidents in Sarajevo during the period 1992 to 1995. He did not personally conduct crater analysis, nor did he determine the calibre of projectiles. Mr. Miokovic led an investigative team which investigated three mortar shells which impacted on Livanjska Street on 8th November 1994. The first impact, at Livanjska Street 26, killed a 15-year-old girl instantly and wounded a 9-year-old boy, who later died of his injuries. Mr. Miokovic and his team inspected the impact crater, videotaped the incident site, and then withdrew, due to the risk of the location being hit again. Less than 30 minutes after the team had withdrawn, two shells struck at Livanjska Street number 36. The second shell killed a 20-year-old woman. The site was secured overnight for investigation on the following day. The investigative team concluded that all three shells had been fired from Bosnian Serb-held positions. Mr. Miokovic also investigated two sniping incidents on 23rd November 1994. In each incident, a tram moving from the old part of town to the new part of town was struck by sniper fire. The second tram was struck about 15 minutes after the first. In the first incident, two passengers were injured. In the second incident, one was killed and three were injured. The investigative team concluded that both trams had been struck by fire coming from the direction of Grbavica, which was under Bosnian Serb control. Mr. Miokovic also investigated an incident on 3rd of March, 1995, in which a tram was hit by automatic gun-fire, injuring several passengers. The gun-fire in this incident was also determined to have come from the direction of Grbavica. That concludes the summary. I'd now like to ask you a very few questions, Mr. Miokovic, to clarify a couple of points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First, in your report concerning the first Livanjska Street shell, which has been admitted, Your Honours, as P1704, your report states that the investigating judge of the Sarajevo High Court, Milorad Potparic, was immediately informed about the incident, and your report says that he authorised members of the centre to conduct the on-site investigation. You recall that report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the first incident that happened on the 8th of November, where, unfortunately, these two children were killed, I can confirm that, pursuant to the legal procedure, I immediately informed the investigating judge of all the facts that I established, and this investigating judge, Milorad Potparic, did not actually go to the scene, as he was obliged to do, sent me to -- he sent me to head the investigation team on the scene on the 8th, and so that is what we did. We went to the -- on scene to conduct an investigation without the presence of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the ethnic background of Milorad Potparic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he is an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is your own ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I am an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How much of your life have you lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: My parents are from Sarajevo. I was born in Foca in 1958, where they were employed at the time. One and a half years after I was born, they came back to Sarajevo. And ever since that time, I have been living in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During the period of the siege of Sarajevo between 1992 and 1996, did you have to leave Sarajevo at one stage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I was injured on the 2nd of June, 1992. Since my condition was getting worse, on the 7th of April, 1993, together with 11 wounded persons, I was evacuated to Germany, and I was in a clinic in a place called Boxtehude, very close to Hamburg. I underwent two surgeries, and I was the only one of those 12 wounded to return to Sarajevo. I returned on the 26th of June, 1993. I wasn't in Sarajevo during that particular period of the siege. For the rest of the time, I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, during the period that you were in Sarajevo for the siege, did you work for the RBiH MUP for the entirety of that period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I have been a policeman from 1987, so I was a police officer when the war broke out. But up until December 1993, I worked as an investigator in a police station, and then in December -- early December 1993, I transferred to the Murder and Sexual Crimes Department of the police in Sarajevo, and I have been performing those tasks ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So it's right, is it, that from -- throughout the siege, you were employed by the RBiH MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you work with other police officers of different ethnic backgrounds during that period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: During that period at the CSB in Sarajevo, of course, if we're talking about the 1992-1995 period, the bulk of my colleagues were Bosniaks, Muslims. This was not a completely ethnically-pure community, but my colleagues of Serb or Croat ethnicity worked in different sectors of the service, as we referred to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court approximately how many sniping incidents you participated in the investigation of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: About 50 of such cases, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in respect of shelling incidents, the investigation of shelling incidents, how many of those incidents did you participate in the investigation of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Also, not less than a hundred, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you the team leader in the investigative teams in many of those incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I was assigned to this section for violent and sexual crimes, in each situation when I or any of my colleagues from that department went to the scene, and the investigating judge was not heading the team, as a rule, the person from that department would be the head of the team. So in each situation where the investigating judge was not present, I would be the team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your investigations during the period 1992 to 1995, did you encounter any credible information that Bosnian Government forces were deliberately shelling or sniping the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Never in any of the cases. I did not see any concrete evidence or operative indications, as we refer to them, nor was I in a situation to have access to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean when you say you were not in a situation to have access to such information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I didn't understand your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I'll repeat it for you. In your previous answer, you said that you "did not see any concrete evidence or operative indications, as we refer to them, nor was I in a situation to have access to such information." Could you clarify your answer a little bit to indicate what you meant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: When I say -- or, actually, when I said something about specific traces, concrete traces on the scene, never on any occasion did ballistics experts or criminal investigation technicians, who were always a part of my team, had any doubts that a sniper -- a bullet or that a shell had been fired from any other positions other than those which at that time were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. When I talked about operative intelligence or information, Sarajevo is not a large town. What I'm trying to say is that many people knew each other. So there were never any rumours, any talks with people, people who were in the armija and even, if you wish, people who were part of the underground, did people who were carrying out regular police assignments find out any information that these things were happening or that anything ever was done in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, that ends the direct examination. I'd now like to deal with the associated exhibits, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Seven of the associated exhibits which are listed in our filing have been admitted. I've provided the exhibit numbers to the Registrar. I can read them into the record, if Your Honour wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I counted six, but you say it's seven, so why don't you name them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly. 65 ter 10439 is P1727. 65 ter 09699 is P1714. 65 ter 13330 is P467. 65 ter 10429 is P1701. 65 ter 09678 is P1704. 65 ter 10437 is D739. Finally, 65 ter 13331 is P1706. And I'd move for the admission of the remainder -- of the balance of the exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections? None. Yes, they will be admitted and given numbers by the Court Deputy, in writing, in due course. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Just to clarify the associated exhibits, all of those admitted previously under seal can be admitted publicly. I just want to clarify that. We're not tendering anything under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, finally, there's one subject I'd like to clarify in private session concerning protective measures, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I saw you nodding, Mr. Miokovic. We need your verbal answer too for our record. So you agreed to only the protective measure of image distortion; nothing else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just waiting for you to finish speaking, Your Honour. Yes, I agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miokovic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Miokovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to help us to clarify your position. Which school did you complete?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a criminologist by profession. I completed the first level of the Faculty of Criminology in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you finish any police school before that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not any police school, but police courses and police training, a number of such trainings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, then? After elementary school, what was your regular education?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I finished the First Gymnasium in Sarajevo, Prva Gimnazija, and after that the first two years of a university education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At which school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: At the Faculty of Criminology in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this faculty established?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think in 1993 or 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how long is this education?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: The university education takes four years. In order to achieve the first degree of this higher education, you need two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if you finished -- if you began your education at that school in 1993, you completed the education in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed that degree -- that title of professional qualification in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may, then, summarise: From 1986, you were -- you had completed the gymnasium and police training courses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't finish police training courses. After completing my gymnasium, my secondary school, I worked on other jobs. I didn't work in the police. In 1987, pursuant to the then legal procedure then in force, I got a job in the police, and I got a job at the Public Security Station Stari Grad, in the criminal police section, where I was working as an investigator, which was quite legitimate. And then while I was doing that job, I completed a number of our own internal police courses about the way to conduct investigations, different ones that I was conducting at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to summarise again. So as somebody who had finished their high school education, you got a job at the police station as a criminal investigator, doing those kinds of jobs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, as you were working, you were continuing your training through internal Police Service courses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you enrolled at the Faculty of Criminology, which did not exist before the war but was opened during the war in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Please believe me that I'm not sure, but I know that I began to work while the war was still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you enroll into this faculty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Two years before I completed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will be making breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in 2003, you enrolled at university; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The time that we are talking about was -- up until that time, you had completed, in terms of education, your high school and a number of police training courses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1993, were you a crime inspector in the Stari Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were from that year onwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Until December 1993, I was working in Stari Grad. In December 1993, I was transferred to the Violent Crimes and Sexual Crimes at the Sarajevo CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And until December 1993, you were working on white-collar crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was working on general crimes, which means thefts, burglaries, break-ins, mostly crimes that had to do with property. I never worked on white-collar crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, you are right. It says that here, "property crimes." Do you remember when Nikola Gardovic was killed in Stari Grad on the 1st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did your station conduct the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the distribution of authority at the time and now within the CSB in Sarajevo, crimes of murder, which this particular crime was, were processed by colleagues from the Violent Crimes and Sexual Crimes Department of the Sarajevo CSB, meaning that the local police station only assisted their colleagues from the CSB who were actually carrying out this task. This also pertains to the subsequent investigation procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order -- for the sake of the parties, would you allow me to remind you that the killing of Nikola Gardovic is actually the killing of the bridegroom's father in a wedding procession near the Old Serbian Church on the 1st of March, which was then followed by the setting up of barricades?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: The place where this incident occurred and the background of the victim is something that I can agree on. As for the assessment whether this was something that prompted the erection of barricades in Sarajevo is a point for discussion, and it's something that I cannot agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's enough for the parties to know that the killing of Nikola Gardovic is actually the killing that is usually referred to as the killing in the wedding procession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you moved to the Violent Crimes and Sexual Crimes Department - I am reading on the second page of your statement - you participated in 12 investigations against unidentified perpetrators, and out of those 12, you managed to solve 10; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: If all this that you said, you said using the plural, "we," as the department, then that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in how many of these investigations were you the lead investigator?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot recall that. It's been a long time since then. But I would like to say that in investigations of crimes, classic murders at that time during the war, during the siege of Sarajevo, that we were conducting, the main person in charge of the activity, the person who was the team leader, would usually be the chief of that department. The rest of us, the members of the department, would be carrying out those assignments, but the co-ordination in that case was entrusted to the chief of the section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did an investigating judge take part as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule and, of course, always in compliance with the then Law on Criminal Procedure in force, and I want to make it quite clear, an investigating judge was involved, either directly or by delegating his responsibilities concerning certain aspects of his job to the chief of our department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the qualification of your chief of department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember, but you can rest assured that this post at that time could only be held by someone with a university degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in most cases that was the university degree in law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you. That was not always the case, not always the Faculty of Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the majority of cases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: In the majority of cases, they had degrees in the faculties that we call Social Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of the 10 investigations, how many of them ended with a trial? And I'm talking about 10 successful investigations of unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: In police jargon, a successfully completed investigation means to bring the case to such a level that it can be forwarded to the Court. So out of the 10, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how did these cases end before the Court? How many of these investigations were confirmed by the Court and how many of them ended in a conviction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: After such a long time, I cannot remember which particular cases we are talking about. Secondly, according to the then and the present Law on Criminal Procedure in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Court is not obliged to report back to the police about the results. Therefore, there are no such records in the police that pertain to that period or to the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are there any records kept about the degree of success of the work done by the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, we have our internal police methods which we apply to measure the degree of our success.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that include also bringing it to the trial? Do you consider a success a case that goes to the Court and ends with a successful conviction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to underline once again that, according to the law in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Courts are completely independent. We have no way whatsoever of following what was going on. We have no way of following how many and what kind of judgements the Courts passed. Of course, I'm talking about the present. If we are dealing with major cases, such as homicide, of course we follow that. Now, I can tell you that since 2003 up to date, 97 murders were committed in the area of Sarajevo canton. Ninety-four were solved, and in three cases we only have indications as to the identity of the perpetrators, and there is not sufficient evidence to pass it on to the Courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we talk about the crime of murder, is it important for the Court that the investigation was conducted by an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, that was an investigating judge, and nowadays, it's a prosecutor. So this is the basic statutory obligation for an investigation to be carried out by an investigating judge at that time and by a prosecutor nowadays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sort of at a loss where we are heading. When are you going to come to the relevant issues in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see, Your Excellency. I have finished with this part, but once we go to specific examples, you will realise my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miokovic, you said, in your statement on page 2, that according to some rough estimates, the events resulted in 11.000 civilians killed in the town of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: According to some estimates, and I say estimates made by the CSB immediately after the war, we estimated, and I underscore "estimated," that the number of fatalities in Sarajevo who, at the time when they were killed, had nothing to do with the front-line, that is to say, were not directly involved in combat, was between 10.000 and 11.000. Now, after we investigated these things or after various government and non-government agencies also investigated it, our estimate proved to be right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask how long we are going to work today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to finish -- we have to rise at quarter to 2:00. We have only 10 minutes left, and my understanding is that there's something to be raised by your legal adviser. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, if we could maybe deal with that at this time, and I don't -- perhaps since we have to leave at 1.45, if we could continue the cross-examination tomorrow and I can address you at this time. That would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that can be discussed in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It can be, although since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It takes time, so why don't we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, that would be fine. So, Mr. President, I think -- I don't know if you've had a chance to see, from a late filing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted it has been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you're aware that we filed our 26th motion for a finding of a disclosure violation and for remedial measures, and I just wanted to call the Chamber's attention to the fact that this includes a request for an immediate adjournment or suspension of the proceedings. So I wanted to make you aware of that at the earliest possible time. The disclosure violation is based upon 14.000 pages received by us concerning the hard-drive of the Pecanac apartment search, and we believe, from the very cursory review that we've been able to make of that material that, like the earlier DVD materials from that same search, it contains information that is necessary for use in cross-examination of ongoing witnesses as well as, unfortunately, some material which should have been used with prior witnesses. So I just wanted to -- I don't want to argue the motion, but I just wanted to make you aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's filed, and we have it in front of us. When do you think you can respond to this motion, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I understand, from the Court's inquiry, it would appreciate the earliest possible response. I can't give you a specific projection at this moment, but we certainly have in mind the Court's interest in a response as quickly as can be managed. If the Court would wish a preliminary or tentative estimate by the end of the day, perhaps we can communicate through your legal officer, and the Court can address tomorrow whether that projection is suitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miokovic, how can you match this figure of 11.000 with the information that 13.000 children were killed in Sarajevo? This is an official stance and declaration by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know where you got this as official information. Secondly, I don't know what the Muslim side is. And, thirdly, in the estimates that we made, which amounted to 10.000 to 11.000 killed people, our assessment was that between 1300 and 1400 of children under the age of 15 were included in that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miokovic, would you be so kind --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have some problems with my headphones. I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher would be kind enough to take a look into the witness's headphone. Do you hear anything? THE COURT USHER: Yes. There's a noise in the headphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Miokovic, do you hear me very well, without any noise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see whether --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was incomplete, so I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miokovic, would you be so kind to tell us what you know about the incidents in which large numbers of civilians were killed or were casualties? Can you enumerate these incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Markale first time, Markale second time, Alekse Santica Elementary School, of course, Vase Miskin Street. So these are the first ones that come into mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people were killed on Vase Miskin Street?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I don't know exactly how many people were killed. But even if one person was killed, and at least 15 were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree in that respect, but we have to establish numbers to compare it with your 11.000. How many people were killed in Alekse Santica School?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I don't know that either. During 1.425 days of the siege of Sarajevo, and that's an official figure, there were days when UNPROFOR counted over 3.000 shells that landed in Sarajevo. So on the average, according to UNPROFOR, the number of shells during those 1.425 days was around 300. So based on that, and due to the fact that Sarajevo was under siege, it is true that the army was shooting at Sarajevo, the army that you were the supreme commander of, and that such a huge number of shells and other ammunition was fired at. And this, unfortunately, resulted in the death of 10.000 to 11.000 residents of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miokovic, I dispute this. So if between eight to ten civilians were killed on a daily basis, and we know that there was a huge number of days in which nobody was killed, this then faces us with a challenge of finding the days when these averages were reached, so when exactly the civilians were killed en masse. If you had 100 days without a single civilian victim, then you have to have another day with 700 victims. Can you give us the dates, as an investigator, and the incidents in which huge numbers of civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I am quite sure that you have the capability to call someone who is an expert in statistics and who can corroborate your data. You are entitled to that. I would like to say that we made our estimates based on our police documentation, and these estimates, as I already said earlier, really coincide with the precisely-determined figures, and this is no secret any longer because it contains full names of the people who were killed during the siege of Sarajevo. No matter how I would like to do that, I cannot give you a specific answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we get these official government materials that you're talking about that can be checked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: I am sure that your request is a legitimate one, but I think that you are addressing it to the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miokovic, with all due respect, I know that I can ask someone who is an expert in statistics. But you have put forward the submission, so how are we going to check this figure of 11.000 civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MIOKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can check it in any way you like. In front of you, you have a man who worked on about a hundred investigations, and in the vast majority of these investigations, the outcome were multiple fatalities. That is all that I can tell you meritoriously with regard to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is it for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just tell the Chamber that we have at least four representative incidents that we have to cover with this witness. The Defence cannot relinquish its request, either, to request the OTP to prove what is contained here and which we are going to try and to rebut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tomorrow, we'll sit in the morning, 9.00. We'll rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 29th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
